title: The Lazy Managers Guide to High-Performing Teams
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain recounts stepping away from work for a few weeks, delegating heavily, and returning to find his team performing better and more motivated. From this he argues that great leadership is about doing strategically less, not about hustle and a packed calendar. He offers seven deliberately lazy tactics: default to asynchronous communication, make 1-on-1s mostly listening, give ownership instead of instructions, standardize routine work with templates and automation, say no more often than yes, be crystal clear and then step back, and recognize wins in the flow of work. The move he makes is to reframe laziness as discipline: systems, simplified decisions and letting go replace busyness. The piece closes by asking the reader what they could stop doing this week to help the team perform better.
points: Time away from the team showed the author that delegation and fewer meetings raised performance and motivation while only his own stress fell.
Defaulting to asynchronous updates protects focus time and forces written clarity, so meetings are reserved for things that truly need discussion.
A single question in 1-on-1s, what is getting in your way, followed by real listening, replaces scripted agendas and surfaces candid insight.
Handing over ownership of an outcome rather than step-by-step instructions yields autonomy and often better, unexpected results.
Laziness here is not vagueness: the manager states what, why, who and deadline clearly and then steps back.
quotes: That was the moment I realized: great leadership isn’t about doing more. It’s about doing strategically less.
Meetings are where productivity goes to die. According to an HBR report from 2022, the average manager spends up to 23 hours a week in meetings.
A lazy manager treats 1-on-1s like coaching sessions, not status updates. She listens, looks for patterns, and responds when she has something tangible to offer.
Instead of saying, “Build this deck by Thursday and cover A, B, and C,” they say: “You own our Q4 strategy update. You’re presenting to leadership. What’s your plan?
Great managers are ruthless gatekeepers. They subtract, not add, until only the essentials remain.
Being lazy doesn’t mean being “vague”. It means being crystal clear and then stepping back.
Recognition is a habit, not a calendar invite. Keep it fast, frequent, and real.
